As of 236 PM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: High pressure will continue to drift northeast of the 
Canadian Maritimes, putting the region in a col (or area between 2 
lows and 2 highs), with little flow aloft or wind direction. To the 
west, a weak shortwave will attempt to push east, but will encounter 
lingering surface dry air, and thus will be shunted west of the 
Champlain Valley. As this boundary works into northern New York 
however, there will be enough forcing off the terrain to sustain 
some isolated to scattered showers and embedded thunderstorms across 
the Adirondacks and perhaps the St. Lawrence Valley. PWATS are about 
0.5" above normal, and with little steering flow aloft, brief heavy 
downpours will be possible. Increasing surface instability to 
1500J/kg based on the current SPC Mesoanalysis across northern New 
York bodes some confidence in scattered convection. These showers 
and thunderstorms will be mainly pulse like storms, that bubble up, 
but dont last long and come back down. There is a lack of any shear 
or strong dynamics so no severe storms are expected, but any 
collapsing shower could innately bring some breezes to the surface. 
With decent PWATs to around an inch to an inch a quarter, briefly 
heavy rain is possible. However, given the recent dry stretch 
rainfall amounts will only be around a quarter to locally half an 
inch.

Showers will wane with the loss of diurnally heating tonight. Should 
a location in the Adirondacks get rain today, chances for localized 
patchy fog will increase. A repeat of today is expected tomorrow, 
though the shower and thunderstorm chances slide a but to the east 
with dry air retreating. Pulse showers and thunderstorms will 
develop in the early to mid afternoon across the terrain of the 
Adirondacks and Green Mountains, and by and large should be 
contained to the higher terrain. However, these showers could drift 
east into the Champlain Valley or eastern Vermont by the mid to late 
afternoon Monday, though chances are only 20-30%. Showers will once 
again wane towards sunset Monday. Should across northern New York 
receive multiple rounds of showers Sunday and then Monday, we'll 
need to monitor these areas for potential of flash flooding, but 
this threat is highly conditional. The Weather Prediction Center 
currently has most of northern New York, outside of the Champlain 
Valley, under a Marginal Risk (Risk level 1 out of 4; 5% chance for 
rainfall exceeding flash flood guidance) for Monday. Northern New 
York rivers could see some small rises, but nothing near bankfull 
with the recent dryness we have had. Better, more widespread rain 
chances are expected by mid week.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A slow moving upper low is still expected to track 
through the region by mid week with chances for persistent showery 
weather into Thursday. The main long wave trough over the Great 
Lakes will shift east into northern New York and Vermont by Tuesday 
with a more established system. A nearly cut-off vertically 
stacked surface low will move into the region with widespread 
showers increasing from west to east Tuesday late morning. 
Trends have continued to favor the center, and subsequently
better forcing, staying to our south over Long Island and 
southern New England which places our region in the northern 
periphery overrunning portion of the system. Tuesday will see
continued diurnally driven showers and thunderstorms with more
widespread coverage than Monday. Pwats look to increase towards
1.5-1.75 inches with around 500-1000J/kg of SBCAPE. These
ingredients could be supportive of heavy downpours, mainly
across the St. Lawrence Valley in New York and Rutland and
Windsor Counties in Vermont, though antecedent dry conditions
may continue to limit these pwat realizations. It is still 
uncertain how far north the more widespread precipitation shield
extends, but right now it is likely that the best precipitation
chances and amounts will favor southern Vermont. Any areas that
see heavier downpours on Sunday or Monday will need to be 
watched. By Tuesday, the WPC has the Marginal (at least 5%) Risk
of excessive rainfall over the entire forecast area. Because of
all these additional showers, thunderstorms, and general 
moisture/clouds around, highs Tuesday will come back down just a
couple degrees, in the upper 70s to mid 80s.

The best chance for widespread showers will be Wednesday. The
low over southern New England looks to occlude with good wrap
around moisture transport off the Atlantic along the northern 
edge of the system. Rain on Wednesday is not expected to be as 
convective as previous days. By Wednesday, chances for an inch 
of rain over 48 hours increase from 50-80% from south to north 
across the entire region. Chances for 2 inches in 48 hours by 
Wednesday night are generally under 20% for the area, outside of
southern Windsor County which is at 55% based on the latest 
NBM. Southern Windsor County will have the best chance for any
